submission.summary:
Reviewed Harold Bennett's (pt-1008) apixaban dosing against the FDA label for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and reduced the dose from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily.

Rationale - label requires dose reduction when >=2 of 3 criteria are met:
- Age >=80: YES (81 years, DOB 1945-02-20)
- Body weight <=60 kg: YES - 128.3 lb documented at the 9/24/2026 post-hospital follow-up = 58.2 kg
- Serum creatinine >=1.5 mg/dL: NO - 1.31 mg/dL on 9/24/2026 (post-AKI, back near baseline)

Important discrepancy flagged: the 9/28/2026 pharmacy consult concluded only 1 of 3 criteria were met and recommended continuing 5 mg BID, because it used the 5/14/2026 flowsheet weight of 63.5 kg and stated that no weight was recorded on 9/24. In fact a weight was recorded at that visit, but in pounds within the vitals line rather than on the kg flowsheet. Converted, it is 58.2 kg, consistent with the documented ongoing weight loss/poor appetite noted at that visit, so the patient now meets 2 criteria.

No other medications were changed. Suggest confirming the weight on a repeat clinic measurement and continuing the planned nutrition follow-up; if weight recovers above 60 kg, the 5 mg BID dose would again be appropriate.

Reviewed Harold Bennett's (pt-1008) apixaban dosing for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation against the FDA label dose-reduction criteria (2.5 mg BID if >=2 of: age >=80 years, body weight <=60 kg, serum creatinine >=1.5 mg/dL).

Findings:
- Age 81 (DOB 1945-02-20): MEETS criterion.
- Body weight: the 2026-09-24 post-hospital follow-up note documents a clinic weight of 128.3 lb (shoes off) = 58.2 kg, which MEETS the <=60 kg criterion. This weight was recorded only in the note's vitals and was never entered into the observation flowsheet (latest flowsheet weight remains 63.5 kg from 2026-05-14).
- Serum creatinine 1.31 mg/dL (2026-09-24): does NOT meet (<1.5). AKI from the August admission has resolved (peak 1.46 -> 1.31).

He therefore meets 2 of 3 criteria and requires the reduced dose. The 2026-09-28 pharmacy consult recommended continuing 5 mg BID, but it explicitly stated "no weight was recorded at the 9/24 visit" and used the older 63.5 kg value, missing the documented 58.2 kg clinic weight. His ongoing weight loss (64.4 kg 12/2025 -> 63.5 kg 5/2026 -> 58.2 kg 9/2026, with poor appetite noted) supports the newer weight as accurate.

Action taken: Changed apixaban from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily (med-1008-01), with the rationale documented in the change reason. No other medications were modified.

Recommend the clinician confirm the current weight on a repeat measurement and have the weight entered into the flowsheet, since the dose hinges on a value that is close to the 60 kg threshold and exists only in free-text documentation.

- Empagliflozin 10 mg once daily — added at discharge, briefly held 9/30 for cost, then started 10/1 per Dr. Okafor after copay assistance (most recent instruction).

Continued unchanged: atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily (inpatient pantoprazole was a formulary substitution only, so home omeprazole retained rather than duplicated).

Not added: cefpodoxime — the 7-day UTI course ended with the final dose the evening of 9/30, so it is not current therapy. Inpatient-only agents (ceftriaxone, enoxaparin, insulin lispro correction scale) were also not carried forward.

No allergies documented, and no interaction or duplicate-therapy issues remain on the reconciled list.

Maria Lopez (pt-1003), 2026-10-01 urgent visit with exudative pharyngitis, fever and positive rapid strep antigen — Group A strep pharyngitis.

Key safety finding: her coded allergy list contained only "sulfonamide antibiotics (rash)," but the outside Valley General ED note from 2019-08-12 documents a history of ANAPHYLAXIS to Augmentin (hives with lip/throat swelling ~30 min after a dose, treated with epinephrine). This had never been added to her allergy list, so penicillin (first-line for strep) would otherwise have looked safe.

Actions taken:
1. Added allergy: Penicillins (amoxicillin-clavulanate/Augmentin), reaction anaphylaxis, criticality high, category medication, with source documentation referenced.
2. Prescribed azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily x 3 days for GAS pharyngitis. Chose a macrolide rather than any beta-lactam (penicillin or cephalosporin) because of the documented anaphylactic reaction. Azithromycin also avoids the CYP3A4 interaction with her atorvastatin that clarithromycin/erythromycin would pose; clindamycin remains an alternative if she cannot tolerate or fails macrolide therapy. No sulfa exposure. No confirmatory throat culture ordered — not indicated in an adult with a positive rapid antigen test.

Note for the clinician: please confirm the Augmentin anaphylaxis history with the patient at follow-up, and watch for symptom response at 48 hours given regional macrolide resistance in GAS (~5-10%).

Maria Lopez (pt-1003), seen 2026-10-01 with exudative pharyngitis, fever 38.6 C, tender anterior cervical nodes and a POSITIVE rapid strep antigen (Group A strep pharyngitis).

Key safety finding: Her coded allergy list contained only sulfonamides, but the 2019 outside ED note (Valley General, note-1003-1) documents that she had hives with lip and throat swelling ~30 minutes after a dose of Augmentin in her 30s, requiring epinephrine in an ED. That is a history of penicillin-class anaphylaxis, so amoxicillin/penicillin (usual first-line for strep) is contraindicated, and cephalosporins are also best avoided given a severe immediate-type reaction.

Actions taken:
1. Added a high-criticality medication allergy: "Penicillins (amoxicillin-clavulanate / Augmentin)" with the anaphylaxis reaction detail and its source, so the reaction is visible on the active allergy list rather than buried in a scanned outside note.
2. Ordered azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily x 5 days for Group A streptococcal pharyngitis, with the indication documenting the penicillin allergy rationale. Azithromycin was chosen over clindamycin for tolerability and lower C. difficile risk, and over clarithromycin/erythromycin because those are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors that would interact with her atorvastatin (azithromycin has minimal interaction). No interaction with her amlodipine or her documented sulfa allergy.

Her other active medications (amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily) were left unchanged. Supportive care (acetaminophen, fluids, gargles) and return precautions were already documented by Dr. Shah.

Worth flagging to the clinician: if the patient does not improve in 48-72 hours, local macrolide resistance in Group A strep is a real possibility and clindamycin would be the alternative. It would also be reasonable to confirm the Augmentin reaction history directly with the patient and consider referral for allergy evaluation/penicillin testing, since a verified or de-labeled penicillin allergy would widen her future antibiotic options.

Maria Lopez (pt-1003), 2026-10-01 urgent visit with positive rapid strep and exudative pharyngitis.

Key safety finding: Her coded allergy list contained only sulfa (rash), but the 2019 outside ED note (note-1003-1) documents a history of ANAPHYLAXIS to Augmentin (hives with lip/throat swelling ~30 min after a dose, treated with epinephrine). Standard first-line amoxicillin/penicillin was therefore contraindicated, and cephalosporins were also avoided given the severe (anaphylactic) nature of the reaction.

Actions taken:
1. Added allergy: "Penicillins (amoxicillin-clavulanate / Augmentin)" — anaphylaxis, high criticality, medication category, with the historical details from the ED note.
2. Prescribed azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily x 5 days for group A streptococcal pharyngitis (IDSA-recommended non-beta-lactam option for severe penicillin allergy). No interaction with her amlodipine or atorvastatin; clindamycin was an alternative but azithromycin was favored for tolerability/C. diff risk in a 68-year-old.

No new labs ordered (diagnosis confirmed by rapid strep). Supportive care already documented by Dr. Shah. Suggest confirming the penicillin reaction history directly with the patient at next contact and counseling her on macrolide completion of the full course.
